definition: Charles Lynn Wayne (February 10, 1943 – November 23, 2024) was an American program manager at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA).
details: He was instrumental in creating the Common Task Method for advancing speech recognition and natural language processing technologies by centering around public benchmarks and datasets, and in establishing Human Language Technology (HLT) initiatives programs at DARPA including TIDES (Translingual Information Detection, Extraction, and Summarization) and EARS (Effective, Affordable, Reusable Speech-to-Text).

explainer.lead: Charles Lynn Wayne was an American DARPA program manager who helped speech and language researchers compare their ideas through shared tasks, public datasets, and benchmarks. His work made progress easier to measure and helped shape major Human Language Technology initiatives.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a class where every student builds a paper airplane, but each uses a different test to claim theirs is best. Wayne helped researchers use the same tests and materials, so everyone could see which designs really worked better. He did this for computers learning to understand speech and language.
tiers.practitioner: Wayne’s Common Task Method is relevant when engineering teams evaluate speech recognition or natural language processing systems: use shared public data and benchmarks so results can be compared across approaches. His DARPA work also included TIDES and EARS, which connected common evaluation with speech-to-text and translingual information processing. A benchmark result is most useful when the task and dataset are genuinely shared rather than chosen differently by each team.
tiers.paperLevel: In plain-text notation, the Common Task Method can be expressed as: shared public datasets + common tasks + public benchmarks -> comparable evaluations of research systems. Wayne applied this approach to speech recognition and natural language processing and helped establish DARPA’s TIDES and EARS programs.

explainer.example: Several research teams build speech recognition systems using the same public dataset and test them on the same benchmark. Because the task and data are shared, their scores can be compared directly instead of each team reporting an unrelated test.
